description: Spanish chronicles vs Nahua accounts vs modern historians — five centuries of shifting meaning.
content_html:
Why Interpretations of 1492 Differ

The events of 1492–1522 have been interpreted very differently across five centuries. An interpretation is not simply a description of what happened — it is a judgement about what those events meant, who was responsible and how they should be evaluated. Interpretations change because new evidence is found, because the societies writing history change, and because the questions historians ask change. The conquest of the Americas is one of the most contested events in world history precisely because so much was at stake: empire, religion, race, identity and memory.

For exam questions about why interpretations differ, you need to focus on the authors themselves: who they were, when they wrote, what evidence they used, and what purpose they had. The “what” (what each interpretation says) is easier but earns fewer marks than the “why” (why they differ).

Key Fact

Interpretations differ because of: the author’s identity and background; the purpose of the account (justification, criticism, commemoration); the evidence available to the author; and the time and context in which they wrote. All four factors matter for the 10-mark Compare Interpretations question.

Spanish Chronicles: Cortés and Bernal Díaz del Castillo

Bernal Díaz del Castillo was a soldier who participated in the conquest of Mexico and wrote his memoir, the Historia Verdadera (“True History of the Conquest of New Spain”), completed around 1568 — nearly fifty years after the events. His account is vivid and detailed, describing Tenochtitlán’s wonders and the brutality of combat with equal honesty. He is often praised as a more reliable witness than Cortés himself, because he had less to gain from distorting the record.

Cortés’s own Cartas de Relación (Letters of Account) were written to King Charles I to justify his unauthorised expedition and secure royal favour. They emphasise Spanish bravery, the justice of the conquest and the need to bring Christianity to the Americas. Cortés routinely minimised his own brutality, presented indigenous peoples as barbaric and his actions as necessary for civilisation and Christianity. These letters are invaluable as sources — but they are advocacy documents, not neutral history.

The Black Legend (Leyenda Negra) was a narrative used by Spain’s Protestant rivals — England, the Netherlands and France — to portray Spanish colonial rule as uniquely cruel and barbaric. It drew heavily on Bartolomé de las Casas’s Brief Account (1542), which had been widely translated and illustrated with graphic images of Spanish violence. The irony is that Las Casas wrote to reform Spain from within; his words were used externally to condemn Spain as a whole. Spanish defenders argued that the Black Legend was propaganda, pointing out that other European colonisers (English, Dutch, French) were equally violent and exploitative but were not held to the same standard. This debate — whether Spanish colonialism was uniquely brutal or simply characteristic of its era — continues among historians today.

Nahua and Indigenous Accounts

The most important indigenous-perspective source is the Florentine Codex, compiled by the Spanish friar Bernardino de Sahagún in the 1570s using interviews with elderly Nahua informants who remembered the conquest. Book 12 of the Florentine Codex contains the Nahua account of the conquest — one of the few surviving indigenous-perspective narratives. It describes the terror of the Spanish advance, the smell of gunpowder, the shock of horses and the devastation of the siege. The Nahua informants do not portray the conquest as a heroic liberation but as a catastrophe.

However, the Florentine Codex was compiled decades after the events, in Spanish colonial conditions, and mediated through Sahagún’s translation and editorial decisions. Historians debate how far the Nahua voices in the codex were shaped or distorted by the friar’s own agenda (he wanted to understand indigenous culture to convert it more effectively) and by the changed political context in which survivors were speaking. It is a crucial source — but its limitations must be acknowledged.

Key Fact

The Florentine Codex (1570s), compiled by Friar Sahagún with Nahua informants, is the main indigenous-perspective account of the conquest. Its limitations include: compiled fifty years after the events; in Spanish colonial conditions; translated and edited by a Spanish friar; informants may have shaped their testimony to suit the post-conquest environment.

Modern Historians: Hugh Thomas and Decolonial Perspectives

Hugh Thomas’s Conquest: Montezuma, Cortés and the Fall of Old Mexico (1993) became the most widely read modern account of the conquest. Thomas drew on a vast range of sources in Spanish, Nahuatl and other languages to present a nuanced picture of all the main actors. He is sometimes criticised by decolonial historians for emphasising individual agency (Cortés’s brilliance, Moctezuma’s miscalculations) in ways that can downplay the structural violence of colonialism and the scale of indigenous suffering.

From the late twentieth century, particularly around the 500th anniversary of 1492, a growing movement of decolonial historians and indigenous scholars challenged the framing of the voyages as “discovery.” They argued that the term “discovery” erases the millions of people who already lived in the Americas and frames the event from a European perspective. From an indigenous viewpoint, 1492 was not a discovery but an invasion, followed by genocide, slavery and cultural destruction. This interpretation emphasises structural injustice over individual stories and links the conquest to contemporary issues of indigenous rights, land ownership and cultural recognition. The debate over what language to use — “discovery,” “encounter,” “invasion,” or “conquest” — is itself a historical argument about perspective and power.
exam_tip_html: The 10-mark “Compare Interpretations” question asks WHY two interpretations differ, not HOW they differ (what they say). A response that only explains the content of each interpretation will not reach the top band. Always address: the authors’ backgrounds and purposes; the evidence available to them; the time they wrote. For example: Cortés’s letters and Bernal Díaz differ because Cortés was writing to justify himself to the king; Díaz was writing a memoir for posterity decades later with less to gain from distortion. Modern historians differ from contemporary accounts because they have access to indigenous sources (like the Florentine Codex) not available to Cortés, and they write without the political pressures of the colonial context.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Interpretations of the Spanish conquest differ because of who wrote them, when they wrote, what evidence they had and what purpose they were serving: Cortés wrote to justify himself; Las Casas wrote to reform Spain; Bernal Díaz wrote a soldier’s memoir; the Florentine Codex preserves Nahua voices (mediated through a Spanish friar); Hugh Thomas drew on multiple sources in 1993; decolonial historians foreground indigenous perspectives.
  • The “Black Legend” portrayed Spanish colonialism as uniquely cruel, partly using Las Casas’s own words; Spanish defenders argued this was propaganda by rival powers who were equally violent.
  • The debate over language — “discovery,” “encounter” or “invasion” — reflects deeper arguments about perspective, power and whose experience matters in writing history.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Florentine Codex as a historical source.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying a feature (e.g. compiled by Sahagún using Nahua informants in the 1570s / contains the Nahua account of the conquest in Book 12 / compiled in Nahuatl and Spanish). Two marks for a developed explanation of its value or limitations.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Bernal Díaz del Castillo's account of the conquest.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• He was an eyewitness who served under Cortés, giving his account first-hand credibility.
• He wrote his Historia Verdadera around 1568, approximately fifty years after the events, relying on memory.
• He is often considered more reliable than Cortés because he had less personal incentive to distort the record.
• His account describes both the wonders of Tenochtitlán and the brutality of the conquest with unusual frankness.
[2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why Cortés’s Cartas de Relación present a favourable view of the Spanish conquest.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies that Cortés was writing to King Charles I to justify his unauthorised expedition and secure royal backing; he therefore emphasised Spanish bravery, the justice of bringing Christianity and the barbarism of indigenous practices, while minimising Spanish brutality; develops with specific evidence (unauthorised departure from Cuba; need to claim royal authority retroactively).
Secure: Identifies reason with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Names a reason with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague statement without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Las Casas’s 'Brief Account' (1542) for how Europeans understood the Spanish conquest.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that the Brief Account, translated into multiple European languages, was used by Protestant rivals (England, the Netherlands, France) to construct the Black Legend of Spanish colonial brutality; contributed to a negative international image of Spain that shaped diplomacy and propaganda for generations; the irony that Las Casas intended to reform Spain from within but his words were used externally to condemn it.
Secure: Identifies consequence with supporting evidence.
Developing: States a consequence with basic explanation.
Emerging: Brief point without development.

practice_questions.text: Compare how a sixteenth-century Spanish chronicler and a modern historian might interpret the conquest of Mexico differently. Explain why these interpretations differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Focuses on WHY interpretations differ (not just what they say). Spanish chronicler (e.g. Bernal Díaz or Cortés): eyewitness; writing in or shortly after colonial context; shaped by purpose (justification, memoir for posterity); limited access to indigenous perspectives; operating within Spanish Catholic worldview. Modern historian (e.g. Hugh Thomas): access to multiple sources including Nahuatl codices and indigenous accounts not available to contemporaries; writing with benefit of hindsight and subsequent scholarship; influenced by late 20th-century debates about colonialism and indigenous rights; no personal stake in justifying the conquest. Clear explanation of WHY these factors produce different interpretations.
Secure: Identifies differences in interpretation with some explanation of why they differ.
Developing: Mainly explains what each says, limited focus on why they differ.
Emerging: Describes one view only.

practice_questions.text: 'The conquest of Mexico is best understood as an invasion rather than a discovery.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the interpretation:
• The Americas were home to millions of people with complex civilisations; calling Europeans’ arrival a “discovery” erases their existence.
• The term “discovery” reflects a Eurocentric perspective; from an indigenous viewpoint, it was an invasion followed by genocide and cultural destruction.
• Decolonial historians argue the language of “discovery” legitimised colonial violence by suggesting the Americas had no value before European contact.

Arguments challenging or complicating the interpretation:
• “Conquest” rather than “invasion” may be more accurate — the term “invasion” implies a foreign attack on a unified state, when in fact many indigenous peoples actively allied with Cortés against the Aztecs.
• Contemporary Spanish sources genuinely believed they were bringing civilisation and Christianity, making “discovery” meaningful within their own worldview even if problematic from a modern perspective.
• Historians like Hugh Thomas argue for a more complex multi-actor analysis that avoids reducing events to a single framing.

Mastering: Sustained argument, agrees AND disagrees with evidence, substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some relevant points, limited judgement.
Emerging: Descriptive, no evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the Black Legend (Leyenda Negra)?
options: An Aztec prophecy about the return of Quetzalcoatl
A hostile narrative used by Spain's Protestant rivals portraying Spanish colonial rule as uniquely cruel
A collection of Nahua accounts of the conquest compiled in the 1570s
The Spanish term for the Aztec Night of Weeping

knowledge_checks.q: Who compiled the Florentine Codex in the 1570s?
Cortés wrote his Cartas de Relación directly to King _____ to justify his unauthorised expedition.
Bernal Díaz del Castillo completed his Historia Verdadera approximately _____ years after the events he described.
Match each source or historian to their perspective on the conquest:
right: Spanish justification for the unauthorised expedition, written to impress the king
Nahua-perspective account compiled by Sahagún with indigenous informants in the 1570s
Late 20th-century view emphasising indigenous suffering and rejecting the term 'discovery'

flashcard_questions.q: What were Cortés's Cartas de Relación?
flashcard_questions.a: Letters written to King Charles I justifying his unauthorised expedition and requesting royal backing.

flashcard_questions.q: Who was Bernal Díaz del Castillo?
flashcard_questions.a: A Spanish soldier who served under Cortés and wrote the Historia Verdadera, a first-hand account of the conquest completed c.1568.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Black Legend (Leyenda Negra)?
flashcard_questions.a: A narrative used by Spain's Protestant rivals portraying Spanish colonial rule as uniquely cruel, partly based on Las Casas's writings.
A post-conquest compilation of Aztec history and culture compiled by Friar Sahagún in the 1570s using Nahua informants.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one limitation of the Florentine Codex as a source for the Nahua perspective?
flashcard_questions.a: It was compiled fifty years after the conquest, in colonial conditions, and mediated through a Spanish friar's translations.
British historian (1931–2017) whose 1993 book Conquest presented the Spanish conquest as a complex encounter driven by personal ambition.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an 'interpretation' in historical study?
flashcard_questions.a: A judgement about what past events meant, shaped by the author's background, purpose, evidence and the time they wrote.

flashcard_questions.q: What four factors explain why two historical interpretations of the same event might differ?
flashcard_questions.a: Author's identity and background; purpose of the account; evidence available; time and context of writing.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do decolonial historians reject the term 'discovery' for 1492?
flashcard_questions.a: Because it erases the millions of people already living in the Americas and frames the event from a European perspective.

flashcard_questions.q: What was Las Casas's purpose in writing the Brief Account (1542)?
flashcard_questions.a: To expose Spanish atrocities and persuade the crown to reform the colonial system — he intended reform from within, not international condemnation.

items.description: Terrence Malick's film depicts the first contact between English settlers and Powhatan people — a thoughtful exploration of encounter from multiple perspectives, directly relevant to debates about discovery versus invasion.

items.description: Set in colonial South America, this film dramatises the tension between Spanish imperial power and indigenous rights through the lens of Jesuit missionaries — relevant to the Black Legend and debates about Spanish colonial purpose.

items.description: Article on the major indigenous-perspective source compiled by Friar Sahagún in the 1570s, explaining its structure, content and significance for understanding Nahua accounts of the conquest.

items.description: Clear explanation of what historiography means — why historical accounts differ across time — directly relevant to the compare-interpretations exam skill.
